title: 37 Degrees — The Normal Temperature That Isn't — 2026-09-01
rationale: This episode is built around a single move: show that "37 is normal, 38 is fever" is not a biological fact but a 158-year-old measurement artifact, then trace what that artifact costs in a modern hospital. The arc runs chronologically and causally — Wunderlich's flawed 1868 methodology (LITFL), its overturning by Mackowiak's 1992 re-analysis and Protsiv's 2020 population-drift data, the clinical harm of applying one number to a moving baseline (IDSA's elderly-specific threshold), and then the pivot the angle demands: once a fever is found, what should be done about it? HEAT supplies the direct trial evidence that reflex antipyresis buys nothing in general ICU sepsis, and the ILCOR CoSTR gives the brain-injury/post-arrest exception real, unpatronizing weight — including the guideline body's own admission that the evidence behind it is weak. Deep-dive format suits this better than debate: the tension between HEAT and ILCOR is real but asymmetric (general critical illness versus a specific neuroprotective population), better explored through investigative unpacking of what each population, each measurement site, and each era of thermometry actually means than through adversarial point-scoring. Fever-as-host-defence and fever-phobia — both named in the brief — are carried by the hosts' own framing around these six citations rather than a seventh source, keeping the episode anchored to its strongest, most explicitly-named evidence. The throughline for the listener: a number born from a foot-long thermometer and 25,000 German patients is still driving triage algorithms and elderly antibiotic decisions today — and a rational policy would use individual baselines and site-specific thresholds, treating fever for comfort rather than as a target.
case_vignette: An 84-year-old care-home resident arrives in the ED with new confusion and poor oral intake. Her tympanic temperature reads 37.3°C — "normal" by the textbook 38°C cutoff the triage system was built on — but she's tachycardic and hypotensive, and her home's own charts show she hasn't topped 36.2°C in a month. The team has to decide whether "afebrile" means "not septic," or whether they're looking at exactly the 1.1°C rise above baseline that IDSA's elderly-specific criteria were written to catch — and that a population threshold from 1868 was never built to see.

sources.title: Carl Wunderlich — LITFL Medical Eponym Library
sources.why: Anchors the whole episode in its origin: a foot-long thermometer, 20-minute equilibration, one million axillary readings on 25,000 patients — and the reveal that Wunderlich's own upper limit was 38°C, later found to rest on flawed, possibly miscalibrated data.

sources.title: Decreasing Human Body Temperature in the United States Since the Industrial Revolution (Protsiv et al., eLife 2020)
sources.why: 677,423 measurements from the Civil War to today show average temperature falling ~0.03°C per decade to ~36.6°C now — proof the 'normal' isn't just wrong, it's a moving target the fixed threshold never adjusted for.

sources.title: IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline — Fever and Infection in Long-Term Care Facilities
sources.why: The direct clinical consequence of one fixed threshold: IDSA defines elderly fever as ≥37.8°C or a 1.1°C rise from baseline, because a single population cutoff misses infection in frail older adults who run cooler at baseline.

sources.title: HEAT trial (Young et al., NEJM 2015) — The Bottom Line critical appraisal
sources.why: The 700-patient RCT at the clinical center of the episode: IV paracetamol for fever in ICU sepsis changed neither ICU-free days nor 28-day mortality — direct trial evidence that treating the number doesn't treat the patient.

sources.title: ILCOR ALS Task Force — Temperature Control in Adult Cardiac Arrest (2025 CoSTR)
sources.why: Gives the genuine exception its full weight — international consensus to actively prevent fever (≤37.5°C) after cardiac arrest — while the guideline body itself labels this a 'weak recommendation, low-certainty evidence,' a candid counterweight to HEAT.
